stem: An adult with a hyperglycemic crisis has profound dehydration and marked hyperosmolality. Which additional finding would most strongly favor hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state (HHS) rather than diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA)?

options.A: Absence of significant ketonemia and metabolic acidosis
options.B: Marked ketonemia accompanied by metabolic acidosis
options.C: Kussmaul respirations caused by compensation for metabolic acidosis
options.D: A mixed presentation with substantial ketonemia and hyperosmolality

rationale: A is correct. The 2024 international consensus report, which remains incorporated into current ADA guidance, characterizes HHS by severe hyperglycemia, hyperosmolality, and dehydration without significant ketonemia or metabolic acidosis. DKA, in contrast, requires elevated ketones and metabolic acidosis. B and C therefore favor DKA. D describes recognized overlap between DKA and HHS rather than a finding that specifically favors HHS; mixed hyperglycemic crises are common enough that the nurse should not rely on diabetes type or onset speed alone to distinguish the conditions.
educational_objective: Differentiate HHS from DKA by recognizing hyperosmolality and dehydration without significant ketonemia or metabolic acidosis as the characteristic HHS pattern, while remembering that mixed DKA/HHS presentations can occur.
source_organization: American Diabetes Association; European Association for the Study of Diabetes; Joint British Diabetes Societies for Inpatient Care; American Association of Clinical Endocrinology; Diabetes Technology Society
source_document_title: Hyperglycemic Crises in Adults With Diabetes: A Consensus Report; Diagnosis and Classification of Diabetes: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026
source_version_date: Consensus report published June 22, 2024; ADA Standards of Care 2026 published December 8, 2025; accessed 2026-08-17
source_locator: 2024 Consensus Report — Introduction and Section 3 ‘Diagnostic Criteria for HHS’: HHS is significant hyperglycemia and hyperosmolality in the absence of severe ketonemia and metabolic acidosis; overlap between DKA and HHS occurs. ADA 2026 Section 2 — HHS is more typically associated with type 2 diabetes and characterized by severe hyperglycemia, hyperosmolality, and dehydration without significant ketoacidosis; mixed features may occur
source_claim_supported: HHS is characterized by severe hyperglycemia, hyperosmolality, and dehydration without significant ketonemia/metabolic acidosis, whereas DKA requires ketosis and metabolic acidosis; mixed DKA/HHS presentations can occur.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing
blueprint_locator: Physiological Integrity — Physiological Adaptation; recognize acute metabolic emergencies, interpret physiologic findings, and distinguish complications requiring emergency management
blueprint_topic: Physiological Adaptation — distinguishing HHS from DKA
correction_summary: Rebuilt the source item to remove overreliance on diabetes type and gradual-versus-rapid onset as diagnostic separators. The final item uses the current consensus-defining biochemical distinction and explicitly preserves the possibility of mixed DKA/HHS presentations.
audit_reviewer: OpenAI GPT-5.6 Sol — Rule 1 clinical audit + adversarial second pass

audit_findings.source_audit: Verified against the 2024 multi-society hyperglycemic-crisis consensus report and ADA Standards of Care 2026. The defining HHS pattern and recognized DKA/HHS overlap are directly supported.
audit_findings.claim_by_claim: A uses the defining absence of significant ketonemia/acidosis rather than an imprecise demographic or time-course clue. No diagnostic numeric threshold is needed for this construct.
audit_findings.choice_A: Correct; it most strongly favors HHS in the stated hyperosmolar crisis.
audit_findings.choice_B: Incorrect; ketonemia plus acidosis is defining for DKA.
audit_findings.choice_C: Incorrect; Kussmaul respiration reflects compensation for DKA-associated metabolic acidosis.
audit_findings.choice_D: Incorrect as the best answer; it indicates a mixed DKA/HHS presentation rather than pure HHS.
audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: Only A specifically favors HHS over DKA. D is deliberately plausible but explicitly represents overlap, preventing a second correct answer.
audit_findings.cueing: All options are physiologic/biochemical features of hyperglycemic crises with comparable specificity.
audit_findings.blueprint: Physiological Adaptation is appropriate because the item tests recognition of an acute life-threatening metabolic pattern.
audit_findings.independent_adversarial_second_pass: Rechecked 2024 updated criteria, mild ketonemia allowance in HHS, DKA/HHS overlap, type 1/type 2 association versus diagnostic criteria, onset-time variability, and second-answer risk. No unresolved conflict remained.
